newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe secondary bond market may boost trading.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe secondary bond market may boost trading.

text.p: Zimbabwe's proposed secondary bond market will open more investment opportunities to foreign investors who are prevented from buying treasury bills, officials and analysts said on Tuesday.

The central Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) said last week it was working towards the establishment of a formal secondary bond market and was considering setting up an association of market makers in government securities.

The bank's assistant general manager for money and capital markets, Rejoyce Zhakata, gave no date for when the secondary bond market would start, but some analysts expect it to be running before the end of 1997.

"It will take a few months to get the legislation in place, and another couple of months to get everything in place and running. We should have something on the ground within a year," one senior manager with a national discount house told Reuters.
"That is the impression we are getting. The market is excited with the idea because it will add competition internally and bring in more players, especially the foreign investors," he said.
Zhakata told a seminar on the subject that current trading patterns on the local primary bond market would have to change before a formal secondary market was established.

She said the RBZ was reviewing a number of key issues impeding the process, including ending or easing the requirement for insurance and pension funds to hold 55 percent of their assets in government primary securities, which has drastically reduced tradeable volumes.
Of Z$10.5 billion ($983 million) worth of government stocks currently on issue, only Z$4.2 billion are available for informal secondary trading, she said.
Current regulations also limit foreign investors to a maximum 35 percent of primary issues of government stocks and forbid them purchasing such stocks on the informal secondary market.
"The current restrictions on the market trading by foreign investors have virtually meant no participation even on the primary market.

"In this regard, the government, together with the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe will review this issue in order to attract and maintain foreign participation in a market where stocks can easily be bought or sold depending on cash-flow needs" she added.

Analysts say trading in stocks on the secondary market has declined over the last five years because holders face capital losses in a market of high interest rates and high annual inflation, both of which peaked above 40 percent in 1992 but have now fallen to around 22 percent.

Zhakata says the development of a secondary market has also been hindered by the range of instruments on offer, saying there was a need to consider introducing new instruments such as zero-coupon bonds and index-linked stocks.

Reg Max, general manager of Zimbabwe's Bard Discount House, says there is also great business potential in introducing mortgage-backed securities, not just to add depth to the country's capital markets, but to enable more funds to flow into a needy housing sector.

The proposal has won solid backing from President Robert Mugabe's cash-strapped government whose ambitious public housing programme is crumbling under efforts to cut high state spending, currently accounting for about 40 percent of gross domestic product.

More instruments, Zhakata says, will also force local investors -- whom she said were currently generally happy to buy and hold securities -- to trade aggressively so as to improve liquidity in the market.

Zhakata says the central bank and the government are currently amending and drafting new banking, securities and exchange acts, and also looking at setting up a central depository to manage the clearing and settlement of transactions in securities as part of their moves to establish a secondary bond market.

The new market would need massive investment in information technology to track transactions, and to standardise trading in various instruments, Bard's Max and other local financial market analysts say.
($=10.68 Zimbabwean dollars)
